items: Seven ways to trade electricity, five kinds of users, one product. Every screen was dense and every number mattered.
UI/UX designer for two and a half years: the trading platform, analytics, the Vidyut AI assistant, a UI kit and the website.
−30% analysis time, −25% design-to-dev time and +20% website enquiries.

blocks.h: Power trading isn’t one market. It’s seven.
blocks.p: GNA runs a CERC-regulated over-the-counter platform where companies buy and sell electricity. Each way of trading comes with its own quantities, rates, time blocks and deadlines.

blocks.cap: Nine product areas share one platform. A trader may touch several of them in a single day.

items.h: Buy power on the right dates
items.p: Needs rate, quantity and time blocks at a glance.
Needs to see what is listed, accepted and still open.
Needs the market beside their own listings.
Needs roles and approvals, not more charts.
Needs companies, admins and status in one list.
One product had to answer all of these without five versions of it.

blocks.text: The challenge: make a dense, high-stakes product feel calm, without hiding anything a trader needs.

blocks.h: One shell for every market.
blocks.p: Scroll through the Buy/Sell dashboard. Each stop is a decision I made, and why.

steps.h: Your listings on the left. The live market on the right.
steps.p: The two things a trader compares all day sit side by side, so nobody flips between tabs to answer “is my offer competitive?”
Banking, RFP/RFQ, Buy/Sell with its four auction types, BESS, REC and VPPA all live here. Switching markets never means learning a new layout.
Quantity, energy rate, type, point of injection, dates and times always sit in the same place. Status chips say On hold, Active or Accepted in words, not just colour.
Edit, ledger, chat, download and duplicate sit on the listing itself. No hunting through menus for the next step.

steps.h: Offers you can compare in one pass.
steps.p: Filters for finalised, accepted, intraday and next-day deals. Each counter-offer shows expiry and credit rating before anything else.

blocks.h: Four choices that kept it calm.

items.chose: One persistent shell with a role switcher
items.over: A separate dashboard for each market or role
items.why: Nine product areas and five roles could mean dozens of layouts. With one shell, people learn the product once. The role switcher at the top changes what is inside, not where things are.

items.chose: Cards for listings, tables for contracts
items.why: Listings are browsed and compared, so they get cards with a fixed grid. Contracts are checked line by line, so the unified ledger groups them by counterparty in a table.

items.chose: Put the clock in the header
items.why: Auctions are won or lost on time. The reverse-auction screen shows a live countdown, the lowest bid and how full the bucket is before you open a single row.
“Verified”, “Rejected” and “Unverified” are spelled out, so a super admin can scan a long company list and nothing depends on colour vision.

blocks.h: A component library first, screens second.
blocks.p: Shared buttons, chips, tables and cards across every flow. Building them once cut design-to-dev time by 25%.

blocks.cap: Pieces of the UI kit, lifted from the live screens: navigation, listing card, status chips, market card, admin actions, counters and the auction countdown.

items: design-to-dev time with the shared library

blocks.h: Analytics that answer, not just display.
blocks.p: Traders and analysts read power-market data across exchanges, products and time. Clearer charts, filters and comparisons cut analysis time by 30%.

pins.p: IEX, HPX or PXIL is the first choice, because every number below depends on it.
Trend analysis, by product, by exchange, real time, buyers and sellers, entity analysis.
Same axes, same three lines and the same weekly or monthly chips on every card, so a second chart reads faster than the first.
Cards stay small for scanning and open up for detail.

blocks.text: Then Vidyut AI: traders ask about prices and forecasts in plain language. Five screens became one question.

blocks.label: After · with Vidyut AI
steps: With the chart that backs it up

blocks.text: I designed the conversation flow, the answer cards and the chart responses, and tested them with traders.

blocks.cap: Vidyut AI as it is introduced on gna.energy.

blocks.h: A website that explains the platform in one screen.
blocks.p: I redesigned gna.energy with a clearer structure, a modern visual language and responsive layouts.

steps.h: What it is, who regulates it, where to start.
steps.p: The hero names the platform, shows the product and says “Regulated by the CERC” before the first scroll.
Eight short benefits beside the product, so a buyer can check what matters to them in seconds.

steps.h: Show the analytics, don’t describe them.
steps.p: The insights platform appears as itself, with real charts and tabs.
What it is, key features, one illustration. Repeated for the OTC platform, Vidyut AI, GNAi, energy management and green transition.

steps.h: Who we are, and what we stand for.
steps.p: The company and its commitment close the page before the footer.

blocks.h: One design language, three products.
blocks.p: A trading platform, an analytics suite and a website that look and behave like one company.

items: Streams dropped in one bedroom every night, and the third floor couldn’t hold a video call. Nobody said the network was broken.
A one-day design-thinking sprint: observe, map, research, define, decide. A home network treated like a product.
A two-node mesh plan chosen from eight scored options, with a before-and-after scoreboard ready. Validation pending.

blocks.text: Implementation and validation pending. Nothing below claims a measured result.

blocks.h: A network that works in one room isn’t a network that works for a family.
blocks.p: Our home runs on a BBNL broadband line and an ISP-provided Syrotech router. It covers some rooms well and others barely at all, and the rooms that matter change through the day.

blocks.alt: The hall TV unit with the router on a shelf

pins.p: On a hall shelf, fixed by where the fibre enters the house.
TV, CCTV monitor and Alexa all depend on it.

blocks.label: Sprint shape · the sprint ends at a decision

blocks.h: The complaints were small. The pattern wasn’t.

items: The show keeps buffering in R2.
The family, again and again, mostly at night
The family, about the third floor

blocks.text: Nobody said “the network is broken.” Put together, the comments described a problem with the space, not the internet plan.

blocks.cap: Speed tests on 10 Nov 2026, six minutes apart. Same plan, same home. The spread points to place, not plan. Which reading came from which room wasn’t recorded, so it’s a symptom, not a cause.

blocks.h: The network stays put. The family doesn’t.

opts.h: Everyone is in the hall, a few metres from the router.
opts.p: Fire Stick on, phones on Wi-Fi. It works, which is exactly why the problem stayed invisible.

opts.h: Everyone splits into R1, R2 and R3.
opts.p: Further away, behind more walls. R2 is where streaming breaks.

items.p: Hall by day, bedrooms by night.
No choosing between names.
CCTV, Alexa and appliances just work.
Fit for video calls, not just texts.

blocks.h: It started with a pencil.
blocks.p: I walked the second floor, the staircase and the third floor, noting the router, the rooms and how the signal felt in each one.

blocks.cap: The original sketch, not to scale. Notes: R2 weak signal, R3 okay-ish, R1 good, kitchen okay-ish, stairs good.

items.cap: Then redrawn to scale at 30′ × 40′, the base for the 3D model.
Third floor: kitchen, WC, R1, hall and the staircase.

items.h: Walls between the router and every bedroom.
Outside, up, and through a concrete floor slab.
The room with the complaints, furthest from the router.

blocks.h: Every wall takes a bite.
blocks.p: The plan became a 3D model of the house. Distance and walls alone already line up with the walk-through notes: R1 good, R3 okay-ish, R2 weak.

blocks.label: Floor
blocks.alt: Modelled Wi-Fi signal across the house
blocks.cap: Illustrative model: distance and walls only, not measured. Green is strong, red is weak.

blocks.h: Six lenses. Four things worth knowing.
blocks.p: Contextual inquiry, site survey, floor-plan mapping, speed tests, technical research and comparative research.

items.p: 2.4 GHz goes further through walls but is slower and crowded. 5 GHz is faster but fades quickly through walls and floors.

items.h: Two floors from one router is a hard path
items.p: Every wall and floor slab takes a bite. Wall and slab materials not yet confirmed.

items.h: Devices may cling to the weaker one
items.p: The Syrotech and a Deco both broadcast. A possible contributor to R2 drops, still to be tested.

items.h: A mesh is only as good as its link
items.p: Wired backhaul is safest; wireless depends on placement. Backhaul quality still to be tested.

blocks.h: Reframing the problem.

blocks.new: “We need the connection we already have to reach every room we use.”
blocks.p: How might we give every room and floor the family uses one reliable, seamless network that follows them through the day, using the connection we already pay for? That reframe ruled out the most obvious idea, a faster plan, before a rupee was spent.

blocks.h: Eight ideas. A tie at the top. Evidence broke it.
blocks.p: Each option was scored 1–5 on coverage, one seamless network, ease, reliability, room to grow and cost. Sprint judgements, not measurements.

items: One unit per floor, one network
Best in theory; needs cable runs

items.over: Buying the three-node kit up front
items.why: Both mesh options scored 24. Starting with two avoids paying for a node before the data shows it’s needed.

items.chose: Keep the ISP router, run the mesh in access-point mode
items.why: The Syrotech keeps routing and DHCP, which avoids ISP support issues. Access-point mode removes the second router layer and the duplicate network.

items.chose: Retire the old Wi-Fi only after verifying
items.over: Switching it off on day one
items.why: Turning off duplicate Wi-Fi scores low on its own but is essential to one clean network, once the new one is proven.

blocks.h: One network. Two floors. No new internet bill.
blocks.p: A TP-Link Deco two-unit mesh. The ISP box keeps the connection; the Deco takes over every bit of Wi-Fi.

blocks.label: Setup
blocks.alt: Network setup today and as proposed
blocks.cap: Today: two networks and two names to choose from. Proposed: one Deco network in access-point mode, a satellite on the third floor placed after a backhaul test, and an optional third node near R2. Not yet validated.

blocks.h: Success gets measured, not declared.
blocks.p: Nothing below has been done yet. The Deco is still in router mode and both networks are broadcasting.

steps: Speed tests in six spots on today’s setup
Phones, Fire Stick, Alexa, CCTV, washer

items.p: Same spots, same method, before vs after.
A full evening without buffering.
A video call holds without drops.
Only the Deco network visible.
Alexa, CCTV and the washer stay connected for a week.
Add one only if a used spot still falls short.

blocks.h: What a router taught me about design.

items: “It buffers in R2” was the real insight. Where and when mattered more than any spec sheet.
The same house has a day map and a night map. Designing for one would miss half the family.
A speed test is a snapshot. Being clear about what data proves kept me from over-claiming.
Mode, placement and retiring the old network are the real design work.

blocks.text: Next: implement, measure, and update this story, even if the data says I was wrong.

items: A pre-launch mentorship platform with no product to demo, no logos and no case studies.
Show the mechanism instead of making claims. The product is about climbing, so the page is a climb.
Ten chapters, built for desktop and mobile. In client review.

blocks.h: No product. No proof. Still has to earn trust.
blocks.p: Lyftrr matches people climbing in their careers with someone a rung or two above them, for six-week, scoped “lifts”. A conventional landing page in its position would have to make claims, and claims from an unlaunched company read as noise.

items.p: Well-meaning, but from outside the field.
A general answer to a specific situation.
Thousands of connections, few introductions.
Serious guidance costs too much to try twice.

blocks.h: The product is about climbing. So the page is a climb.
blocks.p: One night sky runs behind all ten chapters. Scrolling is the argument: by the signup, the visitor has travelled the distance the product promises.

steps.p: Say what Lyftrr does within ten seconds, then offer two doors: one for Risers, one for Lifters.

steps.h: Drawn one fault at a time.
steps.p: Each reason guidance fails gets its own moment instead of a bullet list.

steps.h: One staircase, read from both sides.
steps.p: Climb a rung, or hand one down. The same picture explains both audiences.

steps.h: Floors you climb, not a feature grid.
steps.p: Nudges, tracking and records appear as levels of the same building.

steps.h: One lift is a favour. Twelve is a trajectory.
steps.p: The page zooms out to show what repeated lifts add up to.
Three rungs of indicative pricing, opening with Batch 01.

blocks.h: Every choice traces back to three goals.
blocks.p: Say what Lyftrr does within ten seconds. Read as funded and serious. End every path in a waitlist signup tagged Riser or Lifter.

items.why: Risers are the volume audience, so their button is filled. Lifters are scarce and high-value, so theirs is outlined: present, not competing.
A Riser/Lifter switch and a live engine panel cycling Signal → Gap → Match → Lift → Proof, so visitors operate the product before they’re asked for anything.
A pinned sequence from Day 0 to Week 6 answers “this will fizzle out” structurally, with a start date, an end date and a filed record.
Colours consolidated into one system. The brand gradient appears only where something is live or worth acting on.

blocks.h: Designed for the thumb, not stacked.
blocks.p: Every chapter was taken through 360, 390 and 430 px. Pinned sequences become swipeable strips that tell the same beat. No horizontal overflow at any width.

blocks.text: What would sharpen it: real photography of Risers and Lifters, live waitlist numbers, and the first three completed lifts written up as proof.

items: Shoppers arrived knowing what they wanted and still had to dig through cluttered pages to find the deal.
UI/UX Designer | Graphic Designer, Nov 2022 – Dec 2023, website and app.

blocks.h: Shoppers came with a goal. The page made them dig.
blocks.p: FreeKaaMaal is one of India’s deals and cashback platforms. Users came for one thing, a deal for a store or a product, and cluttered pages, complex navigation and slow loads pushed bounce rates up.

items.p: Dense pages hid the deals that mattered.
Too many steps to reach a store or category.
Page weight directly affected bounce rate.

blocks.h: Shoppers search by store and category, not by browsing.
blocks.p: Inconsistent deal formats made comparison slow, and the coupon and cashback steps confused first-time users. With thousands of offers changing daily, a strong system mattered more than any single page.

blocks.cap: Three ways in, one card, three steps to save. The structure behind the redesign.

blocks.h: From “I want this” to cashback in the wallet.

steps.h: Offers first, then how it works.
steps.p: A search bar and the coin balance at the top, a featured offer, and a one-line “How FreeKaaMaal works” for first-timers.
Trending searches and popular brands appear before you type, because most people already know the store.
Every result looks the same, so comparison is scanning, not reading.
For people who do browse: short stories with the cashback in the caption, and flash sales with a visible countdown.
Cashback available, pending, withdrawn and promo balance as four clear tiles.
Cashback history by order, with status, so “where’s my cashback?” answers itself.

blocks.h: Three changes that did the most.

items.why: Navigation rebuilt around categories, stores and search, so relevant deals surface in a few taps.
A consistent card system on calmer pages that puts the saving first. Thousands of daily offers stay easy to scan.

items.over: Explaining coupons and cashback up front
items.why: Reveal code, copy, go: a simplified coupon and cashback flow on lighter pages, with the result waiting in the wallet.

blocks.h: Clearer paths, measurable lift.
blocks.p: Clearer navigation lifted engagement and conversion, with one deal-card system keeping thousands of offers easy to scan.

items: Brands couldn’t see ROI and creators couldn’t find the right brands. Everything lived in DMs and spreadsheets.
14 days, end to end: research, flows, app UI and a UI kit.
A two-sided app, dev-ready in two weeks and live on Google Play.

blocks.h: A marketplace only works when both sides trust it.
blocks.p: Influencer marketing ran on guesswork. Briefs, approvals and deliverables lived in DMs and spreadsheets, and existing platforms offered no live insight.

items.p: Brands couldn’t see reliable reach or ROI.
Briefs and approvals scattered across DMs.
The right creator was hard to find, and vice versa.

blocks.h: Focus fourteen days on the core loop.
blocks.p: Brief, match, invite, track, pay. Everything else waited. I built the UI kit first, so two weeks produced a complete, consistent product instead of disconnected screens.

blocks.cap: The loop both sides go through. Each step had to be visible to both.

blocks.h: Explore, apply, track, get paid.

blocks.cap: The creator journey: explore campaigns, read the brief, track status, see the money.

blocks.h: Clarity for both sides.

items.why: Creators valued clear terms, deliverables and payout before applying. The brief screen puts all three above the Apply button.
Milestones tracked automatically, from application approved to payout released, so nobody has to ask “where are we?”

items.over: Earnings hidden in a profile tab
items.why: A wallet with total earnings, available balance and every payout, one tap from home.

blocks.h: Blank canvas to dev-ready in 14 days.
blocks.p: Brands got control over campaigns, and creators got a transparent way to collaborate.

items: A leading chemistry educator’s website that didn’t match his reputation, and broke on the phones most visitors used.
Product designer, one month: audit, IA, UI, prototype and a UI kit.
A credible, on-brand home with one clear action: book a demo.

blocks.h: Strong content, weak structure.
blocks.p: Visitors arrived with intent but left quickly: no clear hierarchy, hidden navigation, branding that shifted page to page, and layouts that broke on mobile, where most traffic came from.

items.p: Key content competed for attention.
Important pages were buried.
Where most visitors arrived.

blocks.h: Structure before visuals.
blocks.p: Pages rebuilt around what visitors came for, grouped by what they’re trying to do, with one action available everywhere.

blocks.cap: The navigation, grouped by visitor intent. “Book a demo” is the one action that follows you.
Home on desktop and mobile: who he is, proof of results and the demo button above the fold.

blocks.h: Three decisions that shaped it.

items.why: Pages rebuilt around what visitors came for, with one clear action: book a demo.

items.over: A new look on every page
items.why: A dark canvas with warm orange and yellow accents, applied through a reusable UI kit so every page feels like his.
Responsive layouts designed for the phone first, because that’s where most visitors arrived.

blocks.text: A credible, on-brand home that’s clearer to navigate and easy to extend with the UI kit.

items: One teacher’s content had to serve very different students: JEE and NEET aspirants, Olympiad students and board-exam classes.
UI/UX designer, 2025: the learning platform website.
One platform, three ways in, and a practice question one or two taps away.

blocks.h: Students don’t browse. They prepare for one exam.
blocks.p: A JEE aspirant and a Class 11 student want very different things from the same content. So the site has three entry points, each with its own home page.

blocks.cap: Three doors into the same content. Students pick the one that matches how they study.

blocks.h: Practice, one tap away.

steps.h: Be exam ready, then pick a tool.
steps.p: The NCERT toolbox and two shortcuts, create a test or take a PYQ mock, sit right under the headline.
Line-by-line NCERT questions, exemplar questions and diagram-based questions.
Previous-year questions from JEE Main and NEET to BITSAT, KVPY and AIIMS, each exam one tile.
An exam prep hub, the PYQ bank, a personal learning dashboard, topic-wise practice, progress tracking and doubt support.
Test packages sorted by exam, class or topic, with price, validity and number of tests on every card.

blocks.h: Put practice first.

items.why: Line-by-line NCERT, exemplar and diagram-based questions are the first thing students see, because that’s what they come back for.
Previous-year questions for 15 exams, from JEE Main and NEET to BITSAT, KVPY and AIIMS, each one tap from home.
Test packages sorted by exam, class or topic, with price, validity and number of tests on every card.

blocks.text: One platform with three ways in, built so a student reaches a practice question in one or two taps.

items: A group working in mining, highway tolling, railways, infrastructure, consultancy and software had to read as one company.
UI/UX designer, 2025: home, about, services, projects and contact.
A clear, credible front door that leads with proof.

blocks.h: Six businesses, one first impression.
blocks.p: A visitor from a highway authority and one looking for manpower services both had to understand the company in a few seconds.

blocks.cap: Six sectors, one story: a company that builds and runs infrastructure.

blocks.h: Proof first, then services.

steps.p: Products, years of experience and completed projects sit right next to who JSC is, so the paragraph is backed before it’s read.
Railways, manpower and national highways as a visual carousel with on-site photography.
An industry-focused approach and an integrated business model, stated plainly.
Services and projects listed in full for visitors who know exactly what they need.

blocks.h: Look like the work they do.

items.why: Products, years of experience and completed projects sit right next to who JSC is.
Railways, manpower and national highways shown through real site photography.
Deep navy, light trails and a map texture that match an infrastructure business.

blocks.text: A clear, credible front door for a multi-sector infrastructure group.

items: Bank staff trained between shifts, on their phones, through a site with confusing navigation and no clear order.
Product designer, one month: research, strategy, UI and prototype.
Staff reported a smoother experience, with better retention and wider adoption of training programmes.

blocks.h: Staff trained in short bursts, on their phones.
blocks.p: The Southern India Banks’ Staff Training College trains employees of member banks. Modules had no clear order, progress was hard to track and the site was desktop-first.

items.p: Hard to find and resume assigned modules.
No clear order or progression.
Small text, low contrast, desktop-first.

blocks.label: The learning path I designed for

blocks.h: A college that explains itself.

steps.p: A full-width banner for current programmes, with clear navigation to About, Infrastructure, News and a live-session link.
Member banks shown up front, so staff recognise their own institution.
Programmes grouped into categories, so staff find their module without scrolling everything.
Classrooms, board room, library, hostel and labs as simple filters with a photo for each.
The board and leadership presented with the same calm layout as everything else.

blocks.h: Designed for a banker’s ten-minute break.

steps.p: Comfortable text size and contrast, one column, a clear header.
Facilities as swipeable cards instead of a desktop grid squeezed down.

blocks.h: Design for short sessions and small screens.

items.why: Modular courses with visible progress, so staff always know what’s next.
Simplified navigation that keeps learners moving: a few top-level sections and filters inside them.
Mobile-first, accessible screens that fit a banker’s day.

blocks.text: Staff reported a smoother experience, with better retention and wider adoption of training programmes.
